01
E-commerce clone

AJIO — finding one thing in forty thousand

A fashion catalogue this large lives or dies on filtering. I rebuilt the browse and product pages around the question shoppers actually ask: does this exist, in my size, in my budget, right now?

Role
End-to-end UI/UX
Timeline
3 weeks
Tools
Figma, Maze

The problem

In an unmoderated test with 6 shoppers, four abandoned a search because out-of-stock sizes were only revealed on the product page. People filtered, scrolled, tapped, and then hit a dead end three levels deep.

What I changed

  • Moved size availability onto the grid card, so a sold-out size never survives to the next screen.
  • Made filters persistent and reversible — active filters sit above the grid as removable chips.
  • Replaced the four-step size flow with one sheet that remembers the last size bought.
  • Rewrote the empty state to suggest loosening the tightest filter instead of saying "no results found".

Outcome

In a second round of testing, all 6 participants reached checkout without backtracking. Average taps from home to cart dropped from 14 to 9.

Full case study board — homepage, category grid, PDP and cart
02
Ticketing clone

BookMyShow — the seat map is the product

Everything before the seat map is navigation; everything after it is payment. I focused the redesign on the 40 seconds where a group of friends argues over row H while the hold timer runs down.

Role
UX research, UI
Timeline
2 weeks
Tools
Figma, FigJam

The problem

Seat maps are dense, zoomable and unforgiving on a phone. Testers mis-tapped neighbouring seats, lost track of how many they had picked, and couldn't tell a sold seat from an unavailable aisle at a glance.

What I changed

  • Set every seat to a 44px touch target, with the visual square smaller than the tappable area.
  • Used fill, not colour alone, to separate available, sold and selected — readable for colour-blind users and in sunlight.
  • Pinned a running summary to the bottom: seats, row, total and hold timer in one bar that never scrolls away.
  • Made the timer honest — it warns at 60 seconds and says what happens when it ends.

Outcome

Mis-taps fell from 11 to 2 across nine test sessions. Every tester could state their total before opening payment.

Full case study board — home, listings, seat map and booking flow
03
Concept app

TuneVibe — a player for people who are already driving

Most streaming apps are designed for browsing. TuneVibe is designed for the moment after you've chosen: one-handed, glanceable, safe to operate without reading.

Role
Product design
Timeline
2 weeks
Tools
Figma, Rive

The problem

I logged my own listening for a week: 78% of sessions involved zero browsing — press play, skip twice, adjust volume. Yet the primary screen in most players is a discovery feed.

What I changed

  • Made now-playing the home screen; the library is one swipe away, not the other way round.
  • Sized skip and play for the thumb arc of a one-handed grip, with the scrubber above so a stray drag can't seek.
  • Showed what's next in the queue on the same screen, so skipping is an informed choice.
  • Built a 4.5:1-contrast palette that holds up outdoors at 20% brightness.

Outcome

Five testers completed skip-and-adjust tasks one-handed without looking away for more than a second. The queue preview removed the "what's coming" back-and-forth entirely.

Full case study board — home, now playing, playlists and search
04
Concept app

Food Cravings — the twenty minutes after you order

Ordering food is easy. Waiting for it is where the anxiety lives. I designed the post-order experience to answer the only question that matters: is my food actually coming, and when?

Role
UX writing, UI
Timeline
3 weeks
Tools
Figma, Protopie

The problem

I interviewed 8 regular users. Every one described refreshing the tracking screen when the ETA slipped. The map showed a moving dot but never explained the delay, so people assumed the worst and called support.

What I changed

  • Replaced the countdown with a range — "20–25 min" survives a two-minute delay without feeling broken.
  • Gave each stage a plain-language line, so a pause at the restaurant reads as cooking, not failure.
  • Put the rider's name, vehicle and a call button above the fold, since that's what people hunt for first.
  • Wrote the delay message in the app's voice: what happened, the new estimate, what you can do.

Outcome

In a moderated test with simulated delays, 7 of 8 testers said they would wait rather than contact support — up from 2 of 8 on the original flow.

Full case study board — home, menu, cart, tracking and offers
05
Website design

LifeCare — booking care without a phone call

Hospital sites are usually built for the hospital: departments, accreditations, board members. This one is built for a person who needs an appointment this week and doesn't know which specialist to ask for.

Role
IA, UI, accessibility
Timeline
4 weeks
Tools
Figma, Stark

The problem

I audited six hospital websites. On five, booking was buried under a department tree that assumed you already knew your diagnosis. Body text averaged 13px — a real barrier for the older patients using these sites most.

What I changed

  • Rebuilt the entry point around symptoms and reasons for visiting, with departments as a secondary path.
  • Set a 17px body minimum and 4.5:1 contrast, then tested the booking flow by keyboard and screen reader.
  • Made slot availability visible on the doctor's card — no clicking through to find nothing free for nine days.
  • Kept the flow to three decisions: who, when, and who it's for. Records and insurance come after.

Outcome

The prototype cleared WCAG 2.1 AA on contrast and keyboard access. Three testers over 55 booked an appointment unassisted on the first attempt.

Full case study board — homepage, services, doctors and booking

How I work

First

Watch someone struggle

Every project here started by putting the existing product in front of real users and writing down where they stopped, not where I thought it looked dated.

Then

Name the one problem

I write the brief as a single sentence a stranger could argue with. If I can't, I haven't finished the research.

Then

Build it rough, early

Low-fidelity flows in a day, tested the same week. Visual polish comes after the structure survives contact with people.

Finally

Hand off completely

Components, states, tokens and edge cases documented — including what a screen does when it's empty, slow or wrong.
